cards.title: Copywriting is sales in written form, not content or creative writing
cards.summary: Define copywriting for ecommerce as written sales persuasion distinct from SEO blogs, organic social and creative writing.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to brief or evaluate product page, ad and email copy on an ecommerce store.
steps: Separate your store's writing into two buckets: content writing (blogs, SEO, organic social) which builds audience, and copywriting (ads, PDPs, emails, landing pages) which sells. The source's framing: copywriters write advertorials, content writers write blogs.
Judge copy by one question: does it move a reader toward a purchase action? If a piece is 'beautiful prose' but has no conversion goal, it is content, not copy.

Stop trying to write witty, creative prose for product and ad copy; the source argues the best converting copy is simple, conversational and concrete, written for people reading on a phone between two tasks.

Accept that you do not need to be a strong writer. The source claims you can forget complicated grammar and school essay structure; one-word changes in a headline reportedly produced a 25% conversion lift in her experience.
Keep every asset single-purpose: either give value (educate) or sell. The source says never do both in one email or asset.
Caveat: These are the presenter's opinions from her consulting experience, not tested benchmarks for your store; validate with your own A/B tests.
caveats: The '25% lift from one word' is an anecdote, not a benchmark to promise internally.
Simple copy does not mean careless copy: clarity is the standard, not dumbing down facts.

cards.title: Treat the funnel as a mountain, not a slide
cards.summary: Map every micro-decision between ad impression and purchase because prospects can drop off at any single step.
cards.use_when: Diagramming the path from ad to PDP to cart for your store to find where prospects leak.
steps: Reject the slide metaphor. The source argues marketing is a mountain: the primary conversion goal sits at the top and gravity works against you, so prospects must make a decision at every step to keep climbing.

List the micro-decisions on a single path. For a Facebook ad that means: stop scrolling? read the headline? look at the image? read the subheadline? read the body? click? Each is a place to lose someone.
Repeat the mapping for the destination: landing page hero (stop? read?), offer (care?), form or add-to-cart (proceed?), and every later step.
Recognize that prospects do not all climb one straight route. The source shows many paths up the same mountain, so the same person may enter via ad, blog, or organic social before buying.
Use this map diagnostically: if a step has high drop-off, the copy at that step is failing its single decision, not the whole funnel.
Apply it to ecommerce by auditing your ad-to-PDP-to-cart sequence for one product and marking each decision point before rewriting.
caveats: The mountain metaphor is a mental model from the presentation, not a measurement framework; pair it with actual analytics to locate leaks.

cards.title: Put the customer in the hero role, drop first-person pronouns
cards.summary: Rewrite copy to eliminate I/me/my/about-us framing so the reader stays the hero of their own story.
cards.use_when: Editing any store asset (PDP, ad, email, about section) that talks about the brand instead of the buyer.
steps: Accept the core claim: prospects narrate their own life as the hero; they will not accept your brand as a better hero. Your role is the guide (Yoda to their Luke), never the hero.
Hunt first-person pronouns: 'I', 'me', 'my', 'us', 'ours'. Also flag your company name and product names used as the subject of sentences. The source says people do not care about you.
Flip syntax so the second person leads. Example from the source: 'You can check this out for a flavor of what I'm going to teach' becomes '...for a flavor of what you'll learn.'
Move about-us style navigation labels (Our Story, Our Mission, Contact Us) toward reader-framed alternatives, or at minimum drop the possessive pronoun.
Keep first person only when it is tied to the reader's benefit: 'If you want my personal guidance on your headshots...' becomes 'If you want... then this is the place to be.'
Fix this during editing, not drafting. Draft freely, then run a pronoun pass over every asset before publishing.
Caveat: this is a strong stylistic rule from the presenter; on brand-story pages some 'we' framing may be appropriate, but the sales asset should still serve the reader's decision.
caveats: Takes practice; the source says it took her years to spot the patterns at a glance.
Do not strip so much context that the offer becomes unclear.

cards.title: Use the email outline template to beat blank page syndrome
cards.summary: Pre-build a skeleton for each email with conversion goal, subject, preview text, story, content, CTA and PS before writing.
cards.use_when: Writing any launch, welcome or promotional email sequence for your store and staring at a blank page.
steps: Decide how many emails the sequence needs, then duplicate a skeleton block that many times so you never face a blank page.
For each email, write the primary conversion goal first. There are only two functions: give value (education) or sell. Add specificity, e.g. 'value: watch the tutorial on writing emails.'
Pre-write the subject line as 'Subject: X' and the preview text as 'Preview: X'. Always write your own preview text; the source warns not to let the email tool auto-generate it because it does worse.
Add a bullet skeleton: story (e.g. 'today I want to talk about X'), content (what the email communicates), call to action, and a pre-written PS. The source recommends always pre-writing the PS.
Fill bullets with ideas in any order, not top to bottom; pop in angles as they come, then draft.
Leave rough or dumb-sounding lines in place during drafting and mark them (she changes the text to red) rather than stopping to fix mid-flow; return during editing.
Benefit: you can see the through-line of the whole sequence and how each message functions as part of the whole.
caveats: The two-function rule (value or sell, never both) is the presenter's opinion and may not fit every lifecycle email.
The template is designed for emails but the source says the process generalizes to ads, landing pages and organic social.

cards.title: Let drafts rest 24 hours and edit by reading out loud
cards.summary: Edit copy by sleeping on the draft, then reading aloud until you never stumble, looking for pronoun flip-flops, tangled syntax and repeated words.
cards.use_when: Editing store emails, ad copy or landing page drafts before they go live.
steps: Draft without editing. If a line feels dumb, leave it, mark it in red or drop a note, and keep writing; the source says 'when drafting, no editing.'
Let the draft rest 24 hours, not 10-30 minutes. After a few hours the same text all looks alike; after sleep, you read it as if someone else wrote it.

Read everything out loud. The primary thing you are hunting: any place your tongue trips. You wrote it and have full context, so if you stumble, a cold reader will too and will close or mark your email as spam.
When you trip, fix the line and restart the read from the beginning, repeating until you can read the entire piece aloud without a single mistake.
Also flag: first-person pronouns you can flip toward 'you', confusing sentence structures you would rewrite simply, and repeated words.
The sleep-and-read cycle also lets you spot confusing syntax written by the earlier, tired version of you; rewrite it plainly.
This editing pass is the source's single most important quality check for any copy asset, though her example focuses on emails.
caveats: Reading aloud costs real time; budget for it rather than skipping it on high-value assets.
Fixing a stumble once may not settle the passage; keep re-reading from the top until it is clean.

cards.title: Fix PPC messaging congruency between ad and destination
cards.summary: Match the promise, visuals and language of your ad to the exact page the click lands on so prospects are never surprised.
cards.use_when: Running paid social or search ads to a store page and seeing high bounce or low click-to-purchase.
steps: Define congruency as the source does: two things being the same. If a prospect clicks your ad, the next step must not confuse them.
Reuse ad colors and visual style on the destination page; the source calls this a 'reprise' in music.

Rephrase, don't must copy, the ad promise in the landing hero. Example: ad says 'want to be an actor? here's a complete roadmap to getting booked in network TV from scratch,' and the page opens with 'your step-by-step roadmap to becoming a working actor from scratch.'
Avoid the counter-example: advertising a Spider-Man t-shirt and landing visitors on a generic homepage breaks congruency entirely; they expected the shirt and got your homepage instead.

Check assets for in-asset congruency as well. In the Jake Paul quiz funnel the source audited, the quiz never gave a result and redirected straight to a $57 offer, which contradicted a 'quiz' premise (she compares it to a Buzzfeed quiz demanding payment instead of a result).
Also check cross-brand congruency: an ad running to a warm high-production audience should not land on a low-production template page that clashes with the brand's other properties.
Practical rule of thumb from the source: whatever the ad promises, the first thing the visitor sees should confirm it, even in different words.
caveats: The Jake Paul funnel is a case example, not a universal result; her involvement was a CRO audit, and the outcome claims are hers.
Exact-match wording is not required; congruent meaning and visual style are.

cards.title: Write PPC and social ad creative for scrollers
cards.summary: Build ad copy for short attention: emojis, short lines, one-to-three-sentence paragraphs and reader-focused wording.
cards.use_when: Writing Facebook, Instagram or Google ad creative for a store and needing formats that stop the scroll.
steps: Lead with a pattern interrupt. The source notes video ads perform well and points-emojis and the waving-hand emoji are popular hooks, e.g. opening like you noticed them checking out your thing.

Keep lines short. Instead of five-sentence paragraphs, use one-sentence paragraphs, and keep the first few top lines at one, one, two, one words — the source's example rhythm: 'one one two one I gotta tell you something now three.'
Apply the earlier pronoun rule: avoid making the ad about you or your product; the source reiterates that nobody cares about your brand in the scroll.

Give the ad a clear, single communicated purpose. The source criticizes a Jake Paul Instagram story ad for barely stating what it offered ('hi I'm Jake Paul, swipe up, quiz' was the gist) and for offering no reason to stop.
Check visual contrast against the feed. The same ad showed a pale, blonde presenter in a white t-shirt against a beige house and driveway, which she says will not catch attention.
Match the ad's promise to the next step (see messaging congruency card), since the creative's job is to earn one click, not to close the sale.
caveats: Emoji and format preferences are the presenter's observations of what was 'pulling' at the time; platform performance shifts, so test on your own account.
The Jake Paul ad critique is an audit example, not a measured result.

cards.title: Use the Facebook Ads Library to study live competitor creative
cards.summary: Find and reverse-engineer competitors' current Facebook ads by pulling them up and checking which creatives persist over weeks.
cards.use_when: Sourcing ad creative ideas and hooks for your store's paid social without relying on stale swipe files.
steps: Open the Facebook Ads Library at facebook.com/ads/library (the source notes the interface changes; verify the current path) and search a company name to see the ads it is currently running, including video you can watch and links to their destinations.
Prioritize companies that make their revenue from ecommerce and direct-response social advertising. The source's examples are ClickFunnels and Kettle & Fire bone broth.
Avoid brands buying brand awareness: Coca-Cola, Honda and similar monopolies spend on visibility, not direct response, and the source says even her $12M clients lack brand-awareness budget.
Scan on a cadence: about once a week or twice a month, review the same set of companies to see what gets cut and what keeps running. The source calls it checking on your ex on Facebook.

Treat persistence as the signal. If a creative keeps running for several weeks or months, the source argues it is pulling; if not, Facebook would stop it. At scale, advertisers refresh creative every few days and reach can be cut within 24-48 hours when people dislike an ad.
Pull learnings into your own angles, hooks, formats and landing destinations rather than copying blindly.
This is better than static swipe files because you see currently working collateral live.
caveats: Spend scale of the brands you study may not match yours; small budgets see slower reach cuts.
Tool interface and path may change; confirm before using.

cards.title: Structure a 10-email launch sequence with three phases
cards.summary: Map a launch as email 1 (introduction), emails 2-7 (lessons, repurposed content, testimonials, FAQs), and emails 8-10 (triple close).
cards.use_when: Planning a product launch email sequence for a store drop, new offer or seasonal promotion.
steps: Use 10 new emails as the source's launch structure, plus a resend to unopens of each with a different subject line and preview text (so up to 20 sends, though each subscriber sees fewer).

Email 1 is 'Introducing: [product]'. Expect lower opens because the subject names the product, but the source reports still around 15% opens versus her normal 25-30%+, and openers are highly interested. Make it a strong sales email: tell the problem story, then list everything in the product, close with a CTA and a PS summarizing the problem, the offer and a click-through.

Emails 2-7 draw from four formats, with at least one of each in the source's recommended mix: (a) a quick-win lesson anyone can apply immediately with a soft CTA like 'what's next' or 'reminder'; (b) repurposing existing content, either your own or external, such as a recommended reading list with Amazon links and five-star review highlights, or videos pulled from previous live events; (c) a success email with one long testimonial or several testimonials selected to address specific objections; (d) a FAQ email collecting real questions from chat, email or your Facebook page and answering them all at once. Each ends with a reminder that you are selling and a CTA.

Emails 8-10 are the triple close: three strong sales emails on the final day. She says she invented this by experimenting after a client debated morning/afternoon versus afternoon/evening closes and they chose all three, since time zones make either choice uncertain.

She reports this structure produced multi-six-figure launches and a business that grew to ~$2M annualized recurring revenue in the Jay Shetty case, but treat these as case examples, not promised results.
If you need revenue fast, compress the schedule; if timing is relaxed, space unopens out with breaks.
caveats: Open-rate figures (15% vs 25-30%) are the source's observation on her lists, not universal benchmarks.
Triple close is her opinion and preferred technique; not tested here on your store.
Launch email topics depend on having testimonials, FAQs and existing content to repurpose.

cards.title: Choose launch pacing: aggressive, moderate or relaxed
cards.summary: Match the cadence of new sends and unopen resends to how urgently you need launch revenue.
cards.use_when: Scheduling the timeline of a product launch email sequence for a store.
steps: Aggressive: over 10 days, send day 1's email, resend unopens on day 2 morning, then send day 2's email in the afternoon, and continue the pattern daily. This delivers 20 emails across the list in 10 days; subscribers only receive the ones they did not open.

Moderate: over 20 days, send email 1 on day 1, resend unopens on day 2, then send email 2 to everyone on day 3, resend its unopens on day 4, and continue with spacing. The source's phrasing: subscribers who opened get a breather.
Relaxed: anything over 20+ days, inserting breaks between sends or doing more resends.

Use list size as an input: on very large lists (the source mentions 10,000 up to 600,000 and million-contact databases), by day three thousands of people still have not seen email 1, so repeated unopen resends are worthwhile because you paid to write that copy.
Decide by urgency: the source says choose aggressive if you need revenue in 10 days, moderate if you feel chill; she mostly uses aggressive and moderate.
She reports no meaningful revenue difference between the pacing styles, so treat this as a scheduling preference, not a performance lever.
caveats: Pacing recommendations are the presenter's, and she acknowledges she mostly avoids the relaxed end.
Large-list behavior assumes permission-based lists with unopen tracking; verify your platform tracks unopens correctly.

cards.title: Resend launch emails to unopens with new subject and preview
cards.summary: Increase total reach of each launch email by resending to non-openers with a fresh subject line and preview text.
cards.use_when: Planning launch or promotional email sends for a store and wanting more subscribers to see existing copy.
steps: Treat each new launch email as two assets: the original send and a resend to unopens.
Change both subject line and preview text on the resend. The source pre-writes two subject lines and two sets of preview text when preparing client launches, precisely for this.
If your list is small, she says just changing the subject line is fine; a new subject alone still splits the message.
Recognize why this matters: if only openers see each send, a large share of your list may never see that email; repeated resends recover those people and milk the copy you paid to write.
Schedule resends according to your chosen pacing (aggressive, moderate or relaxed).
Keep each send single-purpose; the resend is the same email, not a new offer.
caveats: Only subscribers who did not open the first send get the resend, so the total audience per send is split, not doubled.
Aggressive resends risk annoyance on small, engaged lists; the source acknowledges this depends on list size.

cards.title: Write the triple close: three sales emails on closing day
cards.summary: Send three strong sales emails on the final day of a launch instead of one, timed across morning, afternoon and evening.
cards.use_when: Final day of a store launch or promotion when you want to capture last-chance buyers across time zones.
steps: On the final launch day, send three separate strong sales emails rather than a single close. The source says she accidentally invented this after a client debated a morning/afternoon versus afternoon/evening close; doing all three handles time zones since you cannot know when people are home.
Keep each of the three a strong, direct sales email; these are the emails 8-10 of the 10-email launch structure.
Use urgency appropriate to the offer deadline: the source frames the triple close as a high-urgency finish to a launch.

Expect this to be high-volume; the source reports it as consistently successful, including in launches she says hit multi-six figures and a business that grew to around $2M annualized recurring revenue (her case examples, not guarantees).
Combine the triple close with the resend-to-unopens mechanic to maximize total reach on the closing day.
caveats: Three sales sends in one day is a strong cadence with unsubscribe risk; the source does not quantify churn.
She describes the triple close as her preferred, experimentally derived style, not a proven universal best practice.

cards.title: Write quick-win lesson emails for the middle of a launch
cards.summary: Use teach-then-soft-CTA emails in the launch middle, capping each with a reminder that the product is for sale.
cards.use_when: Filling the middle days of a store launch sequence with value that keeps the audience engaged without unsubscribing.
steps: Give one small win readers can apply immediately, drawn from something you would write as a blog post, video lesson or tutorial, and make sure it is related to what the product does.
Do not take anyone off the email in the lesson itself; teach the tip fully, then pivot at the end with a crutch CTA the source uses such as 'what's next', 'next step' or 'reminder'.

Write the CTA as a soft reminder that the product exists and has more and better strategies than the one just shared, e.g. 'if you love these strategies, just remember my product is available and has four other strategies way better than this one.'
Finish with a sign-off and a PS that capitalizes on the lesson: name the mistake the reader likely makes, point out the fuller fix the product provides, and link to full details.
Keep the single-purpose rule: this email teaches; the CTA is a reminder selling the product, not a second lesson.
caveats: Soft CTA wording ('what's next', 'reminder') is the presenter's personal crutch phrasing; test your own.
The lesson must be genuinely useful, or the reminder tactic reads as bait.

cards.title: Repurpose existing content into a launch email
cards.summary: Turn prior videos, live events, reading lists or tutorials into a middle-of-launch email that drives clicks to your offer.
cards.use_when: Running a launch sequence and needing email content without writing new assets from scratch.
steps: Inventory existing content: your brands' videos and blogs, external content, or a mix. The source uses this slot to teach while also taking readers off the email and to the content.

Option one, recommended reading list: show the book cover and name, link out (she links to Amazon), and write a short reason it matters, pulled from actual five-star review language. She listed around 10 books this way.

Option two, repurpose prior live content: after a client ran a five-day structured live stream lesson series in a 58,000-person Facebook group, she repackaged that into a launch email because not everyone had seen it.

Option three, topic-focused repurposing: turn existing videos or material into emails like 'five mistakes you're making with your resume' or 'how to network with agents', tying the theme to the product's promise.
Close the email with the same soft CTA framing used in lesson emails ('what's next', 'next step', 'reminder') plus a PS that reminds readers you are selling.
Keep the email single-purpose: one function per asset.
caveats: Repurposed content must relate to the offer, or the CTA feels disconnected.
Suggested reading lists that link to third-party sellers can send traffic off your funnel; weigh that against engagement value.

cards.title: Build testimonial and FAQ emails around objections
cards.summary: Use launch emails 2-7's success and FAQ slots to answer the specific objections blocking purchases.
cards.use_when: Filling launch sequence gaps with social proof and objection handling for a store offer.
steps: For the success email, choose format to fit industry and sales model: either one long, powerful testimonial or case study, or several testimonials.

Select testimonials by objection, not by general praise. The source stresses it is especially powerful when you understand the angles of objection people have and choose testimonials that speak directly to each one.

For the FAQ email, gather real questions from chat features on your site, emails to you, Facebook messages and page comments. The source says review this material for ideas if you do not already know what to include.

Open the FAQ email by acknowledging the questions, e.g. 'over the last few days I've been telling you about my product and you sent in so many great questions I wanted to address them all at once', then answer each question in turn.
End both emails with a reminder that you are selling and a CTA. The source keeps repeated crutch CTAs like 'reminder' and 'what's next'.
caveats: Objection mapping requires you to already know what blocks purchase; do the customer-research step if not.
The presenter's phrasing examples are templates to adapt, not scripts to clone.

cards.title: Use sentiment matching from reviews to mirror prospect language
cards.summary: Read five-star and one-star testimonials to capture the exact internal narrative prospects use to describe their problem.
cards.use_when: Writing store PDP, ad or email copy and needing the customer's actual words instead of brand wording.
steps: Read both 5-star and 1-star customer testimonials. The source's rule is to review both in order to mirror the exact internal narrative prospects use to describe their problems.
Pull phrasing and objections directly into copy: how happy buyers describe the outcome, and how unhappy buyers describe the failure, since both represent the prospect's inner monologue.
Use this research when writing review-highlight email content; she scanned Amazon five-star reviews and paraphrased their language as the reason to read listed books.
Apply the same language to ads, landing pages and product pages to close the gap between how the brand sees the transformation and how the prospect experiences the problem.

Recognize the underlying insight: as the business owner you have full context and passion for the transformation, but prospects come from a totally different background, and your job is to bridge the gap in their words.
caveats: Review language can be raw; adapt the emotion but keep the concrete and specific claims accurate.
One-star complaints may point to real product issues, not just copy problems; fix the product where relevant.

cards.title: Lead prospects from their reality to the primary conversion goal
cards.summary: Account for the gap between the owner's expert context and the prospect's everyday perspective when writing any asset.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why store copy about the transformation fails to land with prospects even though the product is good.
steps: Acknowledge the asymmetry: you are the expert with the full context and passion for the transformation your product delivers; prospects arrive with a totally different background and set of experiences.

Identify your primary conversion goal for the asset (a sale for most stores; for the source's consulting example it might be a free consultation), and write every step toward that goal in the prospect's terms, not yours.
Frame copy so it leads the prospect from where they are to the goal, not from where you are. The source calls understanding this gap 'absolutely key to everything else.'
Apply it across assets: ad, landing page and email should each assume the reader's starting point and move them one micro-decision closer to the goal.

Use your expertise only after connecting to the reader's reality; the source's acting-course example is that people care about her specific frameworks for getting into network TV from scratch, but not until the copy relates them to the reader.
caveats: This is a mindset framing from the source, not a measurement method.
Copy that skips the reader's starting point may still work short-term, but the source argues it underperforms.

Example: ad says 'want to be an actor? here's a complete roadmap to getting booked in network TV from scratch,' and the page opens with 'your step-by-step roadmap to becoming a working actor from scratch.'","Avoid the counter-example: advertising a Spider-Man t-shirt and landing visitors on a generic homepage breaks congruency entirely; they expected the shirt and got your homepage instead.","Check assets for in-asset congruency as well. In the Jake Paul quiz funnel the source audited, the quiz never gave a result and redirected straight to a $57 offer, which contradicted a 'quiz' premise (she compares it to a Buzzfeed quiz demanding payment instead of a result).","Also check cross-brand congruency: an ad running to a warm high-production audience should not land on a low-production template page that clashes with the brand's other properties.","Practical rule of thumb from the source: whatever the ad promises, the first thing the visitor sees should confirm it, even in different words."],"caveats":["The Jake Paul funnel is a case example, not a universal result; her involvement was a CRO audit, and the outcome claims are hers.","Exact-match wording is not required; congruent meaning and visual style are."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","conversion-optimization","landing-page","creative-strategy","paid-social","message-match"]},{"title":"Write PPC and social ad creative for scrollers","summary":"Build ad copy for short attention: emojis, short lines, one-to-three-sentence paragraphs and reader-focused wording.","use_when":"Writing Facebook, Instagram or Google ad creative for a store and needing formats that stop the scroll.","steps":["Lead with a pattern interrupt. The source notes video ads perform well and points-emojis and the waving-hand emoji are popular hooks, e.g. opening like you noticed them checking out your thing.","Keep lines short. Instead of five-sentence paragraphs, use one-sentence paragraphs, and keep the first few top lines at one, one, two, one words — the source's example rhythm: 'one one two one I gotta tell you something now three.'","Apply the earlier pronoun rule: avoid making the ad about you or your product; the source reiterates that nobody cares about your brand in the scroll.","Give the ad a clear, single communicated purpose. The source criticizes a Jake Paul Instagram story ad for barely stating what it offered ('hi I'm Jake Paul, swipe up, quiz' was the gist) and for offering no reason to stop.","Check visual contrast against the feed. The same ad showed a pale, blonde presenter in a white t-shirt against a beige house and driveway, which she says will not catch attention.","Match the ad's promise to the next step (see messaging congruency card), since the creative's job is to earn one click, not to close the sale."],"caveats":["Emoji and format preferences are the presenter's observations of what was 'pulling' at the time; platform performance shifts, so test on your own account.","The Jake Paul ad critique is an audit example, not a measured result."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","creative-strategy","paid-social","copywriting","conversion-optimization","creative-testing"]},{"title":"Use the Facebook Ads Library to study live competitor creative","summary":"Find and reverse-engineer competitors' current Facebook ads by pulling them up and checking which creatives persist over weeks.","use_when":"Sourcing ad creative ideas and hooks for your store's paid social without relying on stale swipe files.","steps":["Open the Facebook Ads Library at facebook.com/ads/library (the source notes the interface changes; verify the current path) and search a company name to see the ads it is currently running, including video you can watch and links to their destinations.","Prioritize companies that make their revenue from ecommerce and direct-response social advertising. The source's examples are ClickFunnels and Kettle & Fire bone broth.","Avoid brands buying brand awareness: Coca-Cola, Honda and similar monopolies spend on visibility, not direct response, and the source says even her $12M clients lack brand-awareness budget.","Scan on a cadence: about once a week or twice a month, review the same set of companies to see what gets cut and what keeps running. The source calls it checking on your ex on Facebook.","Treat persistence as the signal. If a creative keeps running for several weeks or months, the source argues it is pulling; if not, Facebook would stop it. At scale, advertisers refresh creative every few days and reach can be cut within 24-48 hours when people dislike an ad.","Pull learnings into your own angles, hooks, formats and landing destinations rather than copying blindly.","This is better than static swipe files because you see currently working collateral live."],"caveats":["Spend scale of the brands you study may not match yours; small budgets see slower reach cuts.","Tool interface and path may change; confirm before using."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","paid-social","competitor-research","creative-strategy","research","meta-ads"]},{"title":"Structure a 10-email launch sequence with three phases","summary":"Map a launch as email 1 (introduction), emails 2-7 (lessons, repurposed content, testimonials, FAQs), and emails 8-10 (triple close).","use_when":"Planning a product launch email sequence for a store drop, new offer or seasonal promotion.","steps":["Use 10 new emails as the source's launch structure, plus a resend to unopens of each with a different subject line and preview text (so up to 20 sends, though each subscriber sees fewer).","Email 1 is 'Introducing: [product]'. Expect lower opens because the subject names the product, but the source reports still around 15% opens versus her normal 25-30%+, and openers are highly interested. Make it a strong sales email: tell the problem story, then list everything in the product, close with a CTA and a PS summarizing the problem, the offer and a click-through.","Emails 2-7 draw from four formats, with at least one of each in the source's recommended mix: (a) a quick-win lesson anyone can apply immediately with a soft CTA like 'what's next' or 'reminder'; (b) repurposing existing content, either your own or external, such as a recommended reading list with Amazon links and five-star review highlights, or videos pulled from previous live events; (c) a success email with one long testimonial or several testimonials selected to address specific objections; (d) a FAQ email collecting real questions from chat, email or your Facebook page and answering them all at once. Each ends with a reminder that you are selling and a CTA.","Emails 8-10 are the triple close: three strong sales emails on the final day. She says she invented this by experimenting after a client debated morning/afternoon versus afternoon/evening closes and they chose all three, since time zones make either choice uncertain.","She reports this structure produced multi-six-figure launches and a business that grew to ~$2M annualized recurring revenue in the Jay Shetty case, but treat these as case examples, not promised results.","If you need revenue fast, compress the schedule; if timing is relaxed, space unopens out with breaks."],"caveats":["Open-rate figures (15% vs 25-30%) are the source's observation on her lists, not universal benchmarks.","Triple close is her opinion and preferred technique; not tested here on your store.","Launch email topics depend on having testimonials, FAQs and existing content to repurpose."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","email-marketing","launch-sequence","copywriting","retention","conversion-optimization","offer-design"]},{"title":"Choose launch pacing: aggressive, moderate or relaxed","summary":"Match the cadence of new sends and unopen resends to how urgently you need launch revenue.","use_when":"Scheduling the timeline of a product launch email sequence for a store.","steps":["Aggressive: over 10 days, send day 1's email, resend unopens on day 2 morning, then send day 2's email in the afternoon, and continue the pattern daily. This delivers 20 emails across the list in 10 days; subscribers only receive the ones they did not open.","Moderate: over 20 days, send email 1 on day 1, resend unopens on day 2, then send email 2 to everyone on day 3, resend its unopens on day 4, and continue with spacing. The source's phrasing: subscribers who opened get a breather.","Relaxed: anything over 20+ days, inserting breaks between sends or doing more resends.","Use list size as an input: on very large lists (the source mentions 10,000 up to 600,000 and million-contact databases), by day three thousands of people still have not seen email 1, so repeated unopen resends are worthwhile because you paid to write that copy.","Decide by urgency: the source says choose aggressive if you need revenue in 10 days, moderate if you feel chill; she mostly uses aggressive and moderate.","She reports no meaningful revenue difference between the pacing styles, so treat this as a scheduling preference, not a performance lever."],"caveats":["Pacing recommendations are the presenter's, and she acknowledges she mostly avoids the relaxed end.","Large-list behavior assumes permission-based lists with unopen tracking; verify your platform tracks unopens correctly."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","email-marketing","launch-sequence","retention","measurement","cadence"]},{"title":"Resend launch emails to unopens with new subject and preview","summary":"Increase total reach of each launch email by resending to non-openers with a fresh subject line and preview text.","use_when":"Planning launch or promotional email sends for a store and wanting more subscribers to see existing copy.","steps":["Treat each new launch email as two assets: the original send and a resend to unopens.","Change both subject line and preview text on the resend. The source pre-writes two subject lines and two sets of preview text when preparing client launches, precisely for this.","If your list is small, she says just changing the subject line is fine; a new subject alone still splits the message.","Recognize why this matters: if only openers see each send, a large share of your list may never see that email; repeated resends recover those people and milk the copy you paid to write.","Schedule resends according to your chosen pacing (aggressive, moderate or relaxed).","Keep each send single-purpose; the resend is the same email, not a new offer."],"caveats":["Only subscribers who did not open the first send get the resend, so the total audience per send is split, not doubled.","Aggressive resends risk annoyance on small, engaged lists; the source acknowledges this depends on list size."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","email-marketing","launch-sequence","retention","deliverability","copywriting"]},{"title":"Write the triple close: three sales emails on closing day","summary":"Send three strong sales emails on the final day of a launch instead of one, timed across morning, afternoon and evening.","use_when":"Final day of a store launch or promotion when you want to capture last-chance buyers across time zones.","steps":["On the final launch day, send three separate strong sales emails rather than a single close. The source says she accidentally invented this after a client debated a morning/afternoon versus afternoon/evening close; doing all three handles time zones since you cannot know when people are home.","Keep each of the three a strong, direct sales email; these are the emails 8-10 of the 10-email launch structure.","Use urgency appropriate to the offer deadline: the source frames the triple close as a high-urgency finish to a launch.","Expect this to be high-volume; the source reports it as consistently successful, including in launches she says hit multi-six figures and a business that grew to around $2M annualized recurring revenue (her case examples, not guarantees).","Combine the triple close with the resend-to-unopens mechanic to maximize total reach on the closing day."],"caveats":["Three sales sends in one day is a strong cadence with unsubscribe risk; the source does not quantify churn.","She describes the triple close as her preferred, experimentally derived style, not a proven universal best practice."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","email-marketing","launch-sequence","urgency","copywriting","conversion-optimization","retention"]},{"title":"Write quick-win lesson emails for the middle of a launch","summary":"Use teach-then-soft-CTA emails in the launch middle, capping each with a reminder that the product is for sale.","use_when":"Filling the middle days of a store launch sequence with value that keeps the audience engaged without unsubscribing.","steps":["Give one small win readers can apply immediately, drawn from something you would write as a blog post, video lesson or tutorial, and make sure it is related to what the product does.","Do not take anyone off the email in the lesson itself; teach the tip fully, then pivot at the end with a crutch CTA the source uses such as 'what's next', 'next step' or 'reminder'.","Write the CTA as a soft reminder that the product exists and has more and better strategies than the one just shared, e.g. 'if you love these strategies, just remember my product is available and has four other strategies way better than this one.'","Finish with a sign-off and a PS that capitalizes on the lesson: name the mistake the reader likely makes, point out the fuller fix the product provides, and link to full details.","Keep the single-purpose rule: this email teaches; the CTA is a reminder selling the product, not a second lesson."],"caveats":["Soft CTA wording ('what's next', 'reminder') is the presenter's personal crutch phrasing; test your own.","The lesson must be genuinely useful, or the reminder tactic reads as bait."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","email-marketing","launch-sequence","copywriting","retention","conversion-optimization"]},{"title":"Repurpose existing content into a launch email","summary":"Turn prior videos, live events, reading lists or tutorials into a middle-of-launch email that drives clicks to your offer.","use_when":"Running a launch sequence and needing email content without writing new assets from scratch.","steps":["Inventory existing content: your brands' videos and blogs, external content, or a mix. The source uses this slot to teach while also taking readers off the email and to the content.","Option one, recommended reading list: show the book cover and name, link out (she links to Amazon), and write a short reason it matters, pulled from actual five-star review language. She listed around 10 books this way.","Option two, repurpose prior live content: after a client ran a five-day structured live stream lesson series in a 58,000-person Facebook group, she repackaged that into a launch email because not everyone had seen it.","Option three, topic-focused repurposing: turn existing videos or material into emails like 'five mistakes you're making with your resume' or 'how to network with agents', tying the theme to the product's promise.","Close the email with the same soft CTA framing used in lesson emails ('what's next', 'next step', 'reminder') plus a PS that reminds readers you are selling.","Keep the email single-purpose: one function per asset."],"caveats":["Repurposed content must relate to the offer, or the CTA feels disconnected.","Suggested reading lists that link to third-party sellers can send traffic off your funnel; weigh that against engagement value."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","email-marketing","content-repurposing","launch-sequence","copywriting","retention"]},{"title":"Build testimonial and FAQ emails around objections","summary":"Use launch emails 2-7's success and FAQ slots to answer the specific objections blocking purchases.","use_when":"Filling launch sequence gaps with social proof and objection handling for a store offer.","steps":["For the success email, choose format to fit industry and sales model: either one long, powerful testimonial or case study, or several testimonials.","Select testimonials by objection, not by general praise. The source stresses it is especially powerful when you understand the angles of objection people have and choose testimonials that speak directly to each one.","For the FAQ email, gather real questions from chat features on your site, emails to you, Facebook messages and page comments. The source says review this material for ideas if you do not already know what to include.","Open the FAQ email by acknowledging the questions, e.g. 'over the last few days I've been telling you about my product and you sent in so many great questions I wanted to address them all at once', then answer each question in turn.","End both emails with a reminder that you are selling and a CTA. The source keeps repeated crutch CTAs like 'reminder' and 'what's next'."],"caveats":["Objection mapping requires you to already know what blocks purchase; do the customer-research step if not.","The presenter's phrasing examples are templates to adapt, not scripts to clone."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","email-marketing","objection-handling","customer-research","social-proof","launch-sequence","copywriting"]},{"title":"Use sentiment matching from reviews to mirror prospect language","summary":"Read five-star and one-star testimonials to capture the exact internal narrative prospects use to describe their problem.","use_when":"Writing store PDP, ad or email copy and needing the customer's actual words instead of brand wording.","steps":["Read both 5-star and 1-star customer testimonials. The source's rule is to review both in order to mirror the exact internal narrative prospects use to describe their problems.","Pull phrasing and objections directly into copy: how happy buyers describe the outcome, and how unhappy buyers describe the failure, since both represent the prospect's inner monologue.","Use this research when writing review-highlight email content; she scanned Amazon five-star reviews and paraphrased their language as the reason to read listed books.","Apply the same language to ads, landing pages and product pages to close the gap between how the brand sees the transformation and how the prospect experiences the problem.","Recognize the underlying insight: as the business owner you have full context and passion for the transformation, but prospects come from a totally different background, and your job is to bridge the gap in their words."],"caveats":["Review language can be raw; adapt the emotion but keep the concrete and specific claims accurate.","One-star complaints may point to real product issues, not just copy problems; fix the product where relevant."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","customer-research","copywriting","objection-handling","product-page","creative-strategy","positioning"]},{"title":"Lead prospects from their reality to the primary conversion goal","summary":"Account for the gap between the owner's expert context and the prospect's everyday perspective when writing any asset.","use_when":"Diagnosing why store copy about the transformation fails to land with prospects even though the product is good.","steps":["Acknowledge the asymmetry: you are the expert with the full context and passion for the transformation your product delivers; prospects arrive with a totally different background and set of experiences.","Identify your primary conversion goal for the asset (a sale for most stores; for the source's consulting example it might be a free consultation), and write every step toward that goal in the prospect's terms, not yours.","Frame copy so it leads the prospect from where they are to the goal, not from where you are. The source calls understanding this gap 'absolutely key to everything else.'","Apply it across assets: ad, landing page and email should each assume the reader's starting point and move them one micro-decision closer to the goal.","Use your expertise only after connecting to the reader's reality; the source's acting-course example is that people care about her specific frameworks for getting into network TV from scratch, but not until the copy relates them to the reader."],"caveats":["This is a mindset framing from the source, not a measurement method.","Copy that skips the reader's starting point may still work short-term, but the source argues it underperforms."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","positioning","copywriting","customer-research","conversion-optimization","product-page"]}]}
